venues.d: India's most storied hotel, facing the Gateway of India since 1903 — the address every visiting family knows by name.
Serene, glass-walled and faultless on Marine Drive — Oberoi service at the southern tip of the city.
A polished uptown tower crowned by AER, the 34th-floor rooftop — the Four Seasons standard, in the middle of the city.
A soaring tower over Lower Parel with the theatrical Asilo rooftop — St. Regis butler service above the mills.
The modern tower alongside the Palace — the same Gateway views and Taj address, at a lighter tariff.
A lush, art-filled garden hotel by the international airport — the calm landing pad for arrivals and departures.

venues.n: ITC Maratha, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: An ITC grande dame near the airport — Maratha-inspired grandeur and ITC's celebrated kitchens.

venues.n: ITC Grand Central, a Luxury Collection Hotel
venues.d: A colonial-modern ITC house in Parel — well-run, central, and close to the Lower Parel dining scene.
A compact boutique tower on Marine Drive with a rooftop over the Queen's Necklace — the small-hotel sea view.
India's most decorated tasting menu — a ten-course journey through the country's produce in a former textile mill.
A chic, low-lit Kala Ghoda room where sharp cooking meets some of the best cocktails in the city.
A Colaba institution for fifteen years, back on form — eclectic, produce-led global cooking to share.
The modern-Indian restaurant that changed how the city eats — regional dishes, reimagined, ten years on.
A twelve-seat chef's counter above a sandwich shop — the most exciting fine-dining ticket in Bandra.
Niyati Rao's ingredient-led kitchen in a historic Fort building — produce-driven cooking that ignores the rulebook.
The back-alley seafood legend of South Mumbai — the butter-pepper-garlic crab is a rite of passage.
Masaharu Morimoto's Japanese room inside the Taj Palace — the city's benchmark for sushi and omakase.
Contemporary Indian by Vineet Bhatia — the first Indian chef to win a Michelin star (in London) — with the sea at your feet.
The Mumbai outpost of the London dim sum house — glossy, precise and reliably excellent.
Dark, glamorous modern Cantonese in Bandra — the international Hakkasan name, brought to the suburbs.
Mumbai's most glamorous seafood-and-scene restaurant — big flavours, bigger crowd, sea breeze on the terrace.
A joyful reinvention of the Indian mithai shop — traditional sweets made brilliantly, by the Bombay Canteen team.
A century-old Parsi cafe famous for berry pulav — a living piece of old Bombay you eat lunch inside.
The city's beloved home of Gujarati and Mumbai street food, served clean and impeccable in a bright canteen.

The basalt triumphal arch on the harbour is where the city gathers at dawn and dusk, with Elephanta ferries pulling away and the Taj rising behind you. Step out of a Taj suite, cross the road, and the whole postcard of Bombay is at your feet.

Jamsetji Tata's 1903 landmark is still the grand dame of the city, its Florentine dome and cantilever staircase as much a Bombay institution as a hotel. Even if you are staying at the Oberoi, come for high tea at the Sea Lounge or a night at Harbour Bar, India's first licensed bar.

An hour by ferry from the Gateway, these 5th–6th-century rock-cut Shiva temples on a green island are crowned by the colossal three-headed Trimurti, one of the great sculptures of India. Charter a private launch, go early, and have the caves nearly to yourself before the day crowds land.

F.W. Stevens' 1887 Victorian Gothic railway cathedral, a working station moving millions daily, blends stone gargoyles and stained glass with Indian palace forms. Book the heritage tour to climb behind the façade into the boardroom and the star-chamber dome.

The tight grid around Kala Ghoda holds the densest concentration of Bombay's Victorian Gothic and Indo-Deco architecture, best walked slowly with a coffee and an eye for detail. This is the heart of the ensemble that earned the city its 2018 UNESCO listing.

The great Art Deco arc along the Arabian Sea glows into a curve of lights after dark, hence its nickname, and its curving parade of 1930s buildings is part of the UNESCO ensemble. A slow evening walk to Nariman Point, or a drive with the windows down, is the city's oldest ritual.

The city beach at the northern end of Marine Drive where Bombay comes to eat bhelpuri, watch the sunset, and mark Ganesh Visarjan every year. Come at dusk for the sea breeze and the theatre of the crowd, not for a swim.

The former Prince of Wales Museum, a domed Indo-Saracenic masterpiece by George Wittet, holds Indus seals, Gupta bronzes, Mughal miniatures and Chola sculpture across 60,000 objects. Ask about a curator-led private morning walk through the Indian sculpture and miniature galleries.

Since 1952 the city's most storied gallery, where Husain, Souza and the Progressives showed and where the pavement outside still doubles as an open-air art bazaar. It anchors a five-minute cluster of the country's best contemporary galleries.

venues.n: Kala Ghoda galleries (Chatterjee & Lal, Galerie Mirchandani + Steinruecke, Project 88)
venues.d: Within a few walkable blocks sit the galleries that define Indian contemporary art, from blue-chip names to the sharpest young programmes. A morning here is how serious collectors take the temperature of the market.

venues.n: Prince of Wales Museum garden & the Kala Ghoda Arts Festival
venues.d: Each February the precinct becomes a nine-day open-air festival of art, installations, music and design that fills the streets of the heritage district. The rest of the year the leafy quarter rewards an unhurried wander between galleries and cafés.

venues.n: University of Mumbai Fort Campus & Rajabai Clock Tower
venues.d: Gilbert Scott's Venetian-Gothic library and its 85-metre Rajabai Tower, modelled on Big Ben and funded by a Jain merchant in his mother's name, look straight across the Oval Maidan. The interiors, when open, hold soaring stained glass and carved teak.

venues.n: Bombay High Court & the Oval Maidan
venues.d: One of the grandest colonial Gothic courts in the country faces a wide green maidan flanked by Marine Drive's Deco towers, the Gothic-versus-Deco face-off that is the whole point of the UNESCO citation. Cricket on the grass, robed advocates on the steps, pure Bombay.

Behind thirty steps and eight Doric columns, this 1833 neoclassical library holds a quarter-million books and rare manuscripts, including one of only two original copies of Dante's Divine Comedy. The reading room feels frozen in another century, and few tourists ever climb the steps.

A perfect ring of gardens ringed by grand arcaded Victorian buildings, laid out on the site of the old Bombay Green, and a favourite for evening concerts and design pop-ups. The colonnade around it is the most elegant address in the old town.

The 1864 Portland-stone fountain of Flora at the crossroads of the Fort district marks the ceremonial centre of business Bombay. Around it radiate the banks, bookshops and Irani cafés of the old commercial city.

A Venetian-Gothic gem of 1870 with a first-floor verandah of cane chairs shaded by trees, one of the loveliest quiet spaces in the city. Members read newspapers here as they have for 150 years, unhurried by the traffic below.

The city's most famous shopping street, from silver and antiques to street stalls, cotton kaftans and the legendary Leopold and Café Mondegar. Have your driver drop you at one end and browse your way to a coffee at the other.

Bombay's oldest wet dock, from 1875, comes alive before dawn as Koli fisherwomen auction the night's catch in a riot of colour and salt. Since the 2017 St+art project its walls carry striking murals and portraits of the fishing community.

A Norman-Gothic market hall of 1869 whose entrance friezes were designed by Rudyard Kipling's father, still trading in fruit, flowers, spices and imported foods. Go for the architecture and the theatre; the wholesale spice lanes behind are a sensory education.

The famous 'thieves' market' is the city's great hunting ground for colonial furniture, vintage Bollywood posters, gramophones, brass and genuine bric-a-brac. Bring an eye and patience; the best pieces sit above the shopfronts, brought out for serious buyers.

A white marble tomb and mosque set on an islet, reached by a causeway that vanishes at high tide, floating on the Arabian Sea off Worli. The walk out at low tide, past qawwali singers and the open water on both sides, is one of the city's great atmospheres.

Mumbai's most beloved Ganesh temple, its inner sanctum gleaming with gold, draws everyone from film stars to industrialists on Tuesday mornings. Arrange a VIP darshan to bypass the queues and enter with calm at first light.

A seaside temple to the goddess of wealth perched above the rocks near Haji Ali, garlanded and thronged, especially during Navratri. The short causeway between the two shrines is one of the more spiritual walks in the city.

A sacred spring-fed stone tank from AD 1127, ringed by temples, ghats and old dharamshalas, hidden in a fold of the city's most exclusive hill. It hosts an intimate classical music festival and feels a thousand miles, not a few streets, from the towers of Malabar Hill.

Terraced gardens atop Malabar Hill with topiary hedges and a sweeping view down over the Marine Drive arc and Chowpatty. The 'old woman's shoe' at the children's park is a nostalgic Bombay landmark for multi-generational visits.

From the bridge above Mahalaxmi station you look down on the world's largest open-air laundry, hundreds of concrete washing pens worked by hand exactly as they have been for over a century. A ten-minute stop that captures the city's engine of labour in one frame.

venues.n: Dr Bhau Daji Lad Mumbai City Museum
venues.d: The city's oldest museum, a jewel-box of restored Victorian interiors telling the story of Bombay through models, maps and decorative arts. Its exquisite gilt-and-colour restoration won a UNESCO Asia-Pacific award and is a joy for anyone who loves design.

venues.n: Veermata Jijabai Bhosale Udyan & Zoo (Byculla / Rani Baug)
venues.d: The city's oldest public garden, from 1861, a leafy 50-acre botanical garden and zoo that also guards the original stone elephant that gave Elephanta its name. A gentle green outing with children away from the heat and horns.

A genuine tropical forest of 100-plus square kilometres inside the city limits, home to leopards, birdlife, a lion-and-tiger safari and quiet walking trails. A morning here is the surprising green lung of a megacity of twenty million.

More than a hundred Buddhist rock-cut caves carved into a basalt ridge in the forest, dating from the 1st to 10th centuries, with a magnificent chaitya prayer hall. Combine with the national park for a half-day of forest, history and stillness.

A gilded Burmese-style pagoda near Gorai crowned by the world's largest pillarless stone dome, seating 8,000 meditators and enshrining relics of the Buddha. Reached by a short ferry, it offers ten-day courses and drop-in guided meditation in serene surrounds.

A rocky seafront promenade where the young suburb comes to walk, court and watch the sea, past the walls of Bollywood's biggest homes, including Shah Rukh Khan's Mannat. Sunset here is Bandra's answer to Marine Drive, breezier and more bohemian.

venues.n: Bandra street art & Chapel Road murals
venues.d: The old East Indian village lanes around Chapel Road, Ranwar and Waroda Road are a living gallery of murals, cottages and cross-shrines. A morning walking tour reveals the Portuguese-Catholic soul beneath the city's coolest neighbourhood.

A hilltop basilica above Bandstand whose September Bandra Fair draws lakhs of the faithful of every religion. The view over the bay and the quiet candle-lit interior reward a short climb through the old village.

A cable-stayed bridge sweeping across Mahim Bay, best experienced at speed with the skyline of the western seafront laid out ahead. The view back from the Worli side at dusk is the modern city's most cinematic frame.

A tiny Koli fishing village and crumbling 17th-century watch-fort survive at the tip of Worli, surrounded by the gleaming new skyline. The lanes, boats and sea-facing bastion are a photographer's secret and a reminder of the original seven islands.

A striking modernist dome housing a science-and-culture centre, art gallery and planetarium, a good rainy-day or multi-generational stop. Its cultural programming brings some of the city's better classical concerts and talks.

The long suburban beach lined with film-star bungalows and the grand old JW Marriott and Sun-n-Sand hotels, famous for its evening chaat stalls. Come for the promenade, the pav bhaji and the sunset, not the swim.

venues.n: ISKCON Sri Sri Radha Rasabihari Temple
venues.d: A serene marble Krishna temple with beautifully carved interiors, tucked just off Juhu beach, with an excellent pure-vegetarian Govinda's restaurant attached. A calm and easy stop for a family darshan and a sattvic thali.

The sprawling studio complex in the hills of Goregaon where much of Bollywood is shot, with sets, gardens and hilltop lookouts. A guided studio tour, or a fixer arranging a live shoot visit, is a rare window into the world's largest film industry.

The city's spectacular new performing-arts complex, with a grand theatre, an art house and the crystal-lotus Great Hall, presenting world-class opera, theatre and blockbuster exhibitions. The most glamorous cultural night out in India right now, dress code and all.

venues.n: Irani café crawl (Britannia, Kyani, Yazdani, Merwan)
venues.d: The bentwood-chaired Parsi-Irani cafés are a vanishing Bombay institution, from Britannia's famous berry pulao to Kyani's bun-maska and Yazdani's brun. A slow morning across a few of them is the tastiest way to read the city's cosmopolitan history.

venues.n: Art Deco Marine Drive & Oval walking trail
venues.d: The stretch of streamlined 1930s apartment blocks along the Oval and Marine Drive is the second-largest Art Deco ensemble in the world after Miami. A guided walk decodes the sunbursts, ships' rails and 'Indo-Deco' motifs that put this cityscape on the UNESCO list.

A pocket of nineteenth-century East Indian and Portuguese-style timber cottages, brightly painted and threaded with narrow lanes, hidden in the heart of the old city. Designer James Ferreira's home and the annual open-house bring this fragile gem to life.

The modest Malabar Hill house where Gandhi stayed on his Bombay visits from 1917 to 1934, now a moving museum and library with his room preserved. A quiet, humbling hour on the freedom struggle a short drive from Chowpatty.

A guided walk through one of Asia's largest informal settlements reveals a staggering economy of leather, recycling, pottery and textiles, run responsibly with local social enterprises. Confronting and clarifying, it upends every assumption about how the city actually works.

venues.n: Mumbai heritage & food walk (Fort / Bhuleshwar / Khau Galli)
venues.d: A curated walking tour, whether Fort's architecture, Bhuleshwar's temple-and-flower lanes or the vegetarian street food of the Gujarati quarters, is the best way into the city's layers. Private guides can tailor a Jain-friendly, entirely vegetarian route with ease.

A fifty-minute ferry from the Gateway to Mandwa reaches the coast of second homes, Kihim's casuarina-fringed beaches and the sea-fort of Kolaba. This is where Mumbai's families keep their weekend villas; charter a speedboat and make a lazy day of it.

A quiet peninsula of Koli villages, palm groves, an old Portuguese fort and beach shacks, reached by a short vehicle ferry from Versova. A low-key escape for a seafood lunch and empty sands within the city's own limits.
A bar that mines the Indian pantry for its drinks the way its kitchen does for food — one of the country's most-awarded.
The 34th-floor open-air lounge over Worli and the sea — for years the definitive Mumbai rooftop.
A theatrical rooftop above Lower Parel — cocktails, city lights and a scene, at the top of the St. Regis tower.
India's oldest licensed bar, facing the Gateway of India — the most storied nightcap in the city.
Some of the sharpest cocktails in the city, in a chic low-lit Kala Ghoda room that doubles as a fine kitchen.
An all-white rooftop lounge over the Queen's Necklace — the classic Marine Drive sundowner.
